Sub-Saharan Africa accounts for the largest share of this total, followed by East Asia and the Pacific and South Asia. Habitability of low‑lying atoll states ends before the land is physically submerged because salt‑water intrusion contaminates the freshwater lens that supplies drinking water, and repeated storm‑surge over‑wash renders the soil unsuitable for staple crops, making the islands unlivable even while they remain above water [S1]. These environmental thresholds are reached well before total land loss, which is why sea‑level‑rise projections underestimate the timing of displacement [S1].

Compiled from public material on the Australia-Tuvalu Falepili Union (2023), > Fiji's Planned Relocation Guidelines, and the Kiribati "Migration with Dignity" policy. Low-lying atoll states — Tuvalu, Kiribati, the Marshall Islands, Tokelau — face an existential rather than a marginal risk. Mean elevation is typically two to three metres. The binding constraint arrives before submergence: saltwater intrusion contaminates the freshwater lens that atoll populations depend on, and storm surge over-wash makes soil unfit for staple crops. Habitability ends well before land disappears, which is why sea level projections understate the timeline for displacement. The Australia-Tuvalu Falepili Union, signed in November 2023, is the first bilateral treaty to create a mobility pathway explicitly framed around climate change. It provides for a defined annual quota of Tuvaluan citizens — reported at up to 280 per year — to migrate to Australia with access to services, alongside Australian commitments on adaptation assistance and a security provision. Given Tuvalu's population of roughly 11,000, the quota is significant in proportional terms, and the treaty is widely treated as the template that other Pacific states may seek to replicate. Fiji has taken the internal-relocation route instead, publishing Planned Relocation Guidelines in 2018 and a Standard Operating Procedure in 2023, and has already moved several coastal villages inland. The village of Vunidogoloa is the most documented case. The lessons drawn from these moves are consistent: land tenure at the destination is harder to resolve than construction; relocation severs access to fishing grounds and ancestral burial sites, which communities weigh heavily; and moves that were community-led have held up better than moves that were state-directed. Kiribati's "Migration with Dignity" policy takes a third approach — investing in education and skills so that citizens migrate as qualified workers under existing labour schemes rather than as future claimants for emergency admission. Across all three approaches, the recurring political objection is that planned relocation can be read as conceding the loss of statehood, which weakens a state's negotiating position in climate finance and loss-and-damage forums.

# Legal status of people displaced by climate impacts > Course demo note. Summarised from UNHCR guidance and the UN Human Rights Committee's views in > Teitiota v New Zealand (CCPR/C/127/D/2728/2016, 2020). There is no "climate refugee" status in international law. The 1951 Refugee Convention defines a refugee by a well-founded fear of persecution on grounds of race, religion, nationality, political opinion or membership of a particular social group. Environmental degradation is not among them, and UNHCR itself avoids the term "climate refugee", preferring "persons displaced in the context of disasters and climate change". The consequence is a protection gap. Someone who crosses a border because their island is becoming uninhabitable generally has no automatic legal claim to admission or non-return, whereas someone fleeing persecution does. Most climate-related displacement is in any case internal, which places it under national jurisdiction and the Guiding Principles on Internal Displacement — a soft-law instrument rather than a binding treaty. The Teitiota case (2020) is the most important development. Ioane Teitiota, a Kiribati national, challenged his removal from New Zealand on the grounds that sea level rise made return unsafe. The UN Human Rights Committee found that New Zealand had not violated his right to life in that specific case, because the danger was not sufficiently imminent. But it accepted the underlying principle: that climate impacts can, in principle, trigger non-refoulement obligations where they expose an individual to a real risk to life or to cruel treatment. It also observed that whole-country conditions could become incompatible with the right to life before territory is physically submerged. Regional instruments go further than the global regime. The African Union's 2009 Kampala Convention is the only binding regional treaty covering internal displacement, and it explicitly includes displacement caused by natural and human-made disasters. The Nansen Initiative and its successor, the Platform on Disaster Displacement, produced a Protection Agenda endorsed by over 100 states, but it is non-binding and works by encouraging temporary protection and humanitarian visa practice rather than by creating status.

# Response mechanisms, finance and early warning > Course demo note. Compiled from public UNFCCC, UN and Green Climate Fund material. Three institutional mechanisms matter for climate displacement response. The Warsaw International Mechanism for Loss and Damage, established in 2013, created the Task Force on Displacement, whose 2018 recommendations are the main formal UNFCCC guidance on human mobility. The loss and damage fund agreed at COP27 in 2022 and operationalised at COP28 in 2023 is the funding instrument attached to this track. Pledges announced at COP28 were on the order of several hundred million US dollars, which is orders of magnitude below the loss and damage cost estimates in the academic literature, generally quoted in the hundreds of billions per year by 2030. Early warning is the highest-leverage intervention in cost-benefit terms. The UN's "Early Warnings for All" initiative, launched in 2022, targets universal coverage by the end of 2027, on the basis that a substantial share of the global population — particularly in Africa and small island developing states — remains outside effective multi-hazard warning coverage. Evaluations of early warning investment consistently report benefit-cost ratios well above one, and Bangladesh's cyclone programme is the standard illustration. Anticipatory action is the operational development that follows from better forecasting. Instead of funding a response after a disaster is declared, pre-agreed triggers release funds before the hazard arrives, allowing evacuation support and cash transfers to reach households in the window when they can still act. Pilots run by OCHA and the Red Cross movement in Bangladesh, Somalia and Nepal report that pre-arrival cash reduces distress asset sales and shortens displacement duration. The persistent structural gap is that finance is organised around either emergency humanitarian response or long-horizon adaptation, while planned relocation sits between the two. Relocation needs multi-year funding for land acquisition, tenure resolution and livelihood reconstruction — a profile that neither humanitarian appeal cycles nor adaptation project finance is designed to provide.

# Bangladesh: delta exposure and the Dhaka corridor > Course demo note. Compiled from IOM, IDMC and World Bank material on Bangladesh. Bangladesh sits on the Ganges-Brahmaputra-Meghna delta, with roughly two-thirds of its territory less than five metres above sea level. Its exposure combines four hazards that interact: tropical cyclones in the Bay of Bengal, monsoon river flooding, riverbank erosion, and saline intrusion into coastal groundwater and soils. Riverbank erosion is the most underrated driver. Unlike a cyclone, it destroys land permanently and produces displacement that is by definition non-returnable, since there is no home site to go back to. Saline intrusion works differently again: it does not destroy land but degrades it, cutting rice yields and drinking water availability until agricultural livelihoods stop being viable. Households typically respond with staged movement — first sending one member to a city, then relocating fully — which makes the displacement statistically invisible to systems that count sudden movement events. The dominant destination corridor is coastal district to Dhaka, with Chattogram as the secondary destination. A frequently cited estimate holds that on the order of 2,000 people arrive in Dhaka each day from rural areas, a substantial share of them from climate-affected districts, although attributing any individual move solely to climate is not methodologically possible. Arrivals concentrate in informal settlements that are themselves flood-prone, producing displacement into a second exposure. Bangladesh is also cited as an early-warning success case. Cyclone Bhola in 1970 killed on the order of 300,000 people; comparable recent cyclones have produced death tolls in the tens or low hundreds, after decades of investment in cyclone shelters, volunteer warning networks and evacuation planning. The displacement count went up while the death count went down, which is the clearest illustration of why a high evacuation-driven displacement figure must not be read as a policy failure.

# IPCC AR6 findings relevant to displacement > Course demo note. Summarised from IPCC Sixth Assessment Report, Working Group II, > "Climate Change 2022: Impacts, Adaptation and Vulnerability". Source: https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg2/ The IPCC's Sixth Assessment Report treats displacement and involuntary migration as an observed impact of climate change, not only a projected one, and states with high confidence that climate and weather extremes are increasingly driving displacement across all inhabited regions, with small island states and low-lying coastal areas disproportionately affected. On exposure, AR6 reports that around one billion people are projected to live in low-lying coastal zones at risk from coastal-specific climate hazards by mid-century. Sea level rise is described as committed over centuries to millennia regardless of near-term emissions, which means coastal displacement pressure continues to build even under strong mitigation — mitigation changes the rate, not the direction. AR6 gives substantial weight to vulnerability rather than hazard alone. It estimates that roughly 3.3 to 3.6 billion people live in contexts highly vulnerable to climate change, and it is explicit that vulnerability is driven by governance, inequality and development patterns rather than by exposure alone. The practical implication for displacement analysis is that a hazard map is not a risk map: two regions with identical flood exposure can produce very different displacement outcomes. The report also introduces "soft" and "hard" adaptation limits. A soft limit is reached when options exist but are not accessible for financial or institutional reasons; a hard limit is reached when no adaptation option can avoid intolerable risk. Displacement is the outcome once hard limits are reached, and AR6 notes that some small island and coastal systems are already approaching them. The report is careful not to endorse specific global migration forecasts, assessing confidence in such aggregate numbers as low because they depend heavily on socioeconomic assumptions.
